method_note: Primary Arabic used for Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi, and Saadi. Jalalayn and attrib. Ibn Abbas are English-only in the live dataset. Competing duration, caller-identity, sariy, and silence-vow interpretations are preserved without harmonization.

propositions.statement_en: Al-Qurtubi prefers the view attributed to Ibn Abbas that Mary's pregnancy and delivery followed immediately, arguing that the withdrawal is mentioned directly after conception.
Ibn Kathir calls the immediate-pregnancy-and-delivery report strange and prefers the apparent, well-known view that Mary carried Jesus as women ordinarily carry their children.
Ibn Kathir reports the well-known majority view that Mary's pregnancy lasted nine months.
Ibn Kathir reports Ikrimah's view that Mary's pregnancy lasted eight months.
The attributed Ibn Abbas entry presents two possibilities for Mary's pregnancy: nine months or one day.
Jalalayn states that conception, fetal formation, and delivery all occurred within one hour.
Al-Qurtubi explains Mary's withdrawal to a distant place as flight from her people's reproach for giving birth without a husband.
Al-Sa'di explains Mary's withdrawal as motivated by fear of scandal after becoming pregnant with Jesus.
Ibn Kathir takes Mary's wish for death as evidence that wishing for death is permissible when facing religious trial or tribulation.

Al-Qurtubi says Mary wished for death for religious reasons—fear for her own religious standing and fear that others would fall into slander because of her—and concludes that wishing for death can be permissible on that basis.
Al-Sa'di says Mary's wish for death arose from severe distress, but that there was no good or benefit in the wish itself; the good lay in what God had decreed to occur.
Al-Tabari explicitly prefers Jesus as the one who called to Mary from beneath her in 19:24, arguing from the nearer antecedent and Mary's later pointing to him.
Al-Qurtubi prefers Gabriel as the caller from beneath Mary in 19:24, while recording Jesus as an alternative.
Al-Sa'di identifies the caller who reassured Mary from beneath her as the angel.
Jalalayn explicitly identifies Gabriel as the caller from beneath Mary in 19:24.
Ibn Kathir reports an Ibn Abbas line of interpretation identifying Gabriel as the caller and saying Jesus did not speak until Mary brought him to her people.
Ibn Kathir also reports the competing view that Jesus was the caller, noting that Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarir preferred it.
Ibn Kathir prefers the interpretation of sariy in 19:24 as a small river or stream rather than Jesus.
Al-Tabari prefers sariy in 19:24 to mean a small stream, reasoning that the following commands give Mary food from the dates and drink from the water.
Al-Sa'di interprets sariy as a river from which Mary could drink.

Al-Qurtubi records both the interpretation of sariy as Jesus, a noble man, and the majority interpretation as a nearby channel of water, without clearly adjudicating between those two lexical senses in this passage.
Jalalayn interprets sariy as a watercourse whose water had dried up and was restored for Mary.
Al-Qurtubi uses Mary's command to shake the palm trunk to argue that seeking provision through effort is God's norm for His servants and does not contradict reliance upon God.
Al-Tabari judges three principal readings of the verb describing the falling dates in 19:25 to be close in meaning and all acceptable recitations.
Ibn Kathir considers it apparent that the palm was a living tree but outside its fruiting season, making the provision of fresh dates a divine favor to Mary.
Ibn Kathir interprets Mary's instruction to 'say' she had vowed a fast as communication by gesture rather than spoken words, so as not to contradict her vow not to speak.
Al-Qurtubi says the apparent meaning, and the majority view, is that Mary was permitted to utter the words of the vow, while another group understood 'say' as gesturing rather than speaking.

Al-Sa'di interprets Mary's vow as silence communicated by gesture and explains that her vindication was intentionally deferred to the miraculous speech of Jesus in the cradle because ordinary denial would not have been believed.
Al-Tabari interprets the vowed 'fast' in 19:26 as silence from human speech and preserves reports that this abstention was part of fasting practice among the Children of Israel.

evidence_links.semantic_link_note: Two Tabari routes preserve the Ibn Abbas report underlying Qurtubi's preferred immediate-delivery reading.
Mujahid is one of the named early authorities for the Jesus-as-caller interpretation preferred by Tabari.
The Ibn Abbas report supplies the Gabriel-as-caller line preserved by Ibn Kathir.
The al-Bara report supports the stream meaning that Tabari ultimately prefers for sariy.
Ibn Kathir also cites the al-Bara stream gloss before preferring the stream interpretation.
